definition: Indefatigable means never tiring; persisting without rest.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word indefatigable. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know indefatigable should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Reporters assigned to the indefatigable senator work in relays: four town halls, two factory tours, and a late-night diner stop, all inside a single Monday.
Energetic says the tank is full this morning and promises nothing about tonight; indefatigable promises the whole season — the tank never empties.
The persistent keep going through setbacks, tired or not; indefatigable goes further — the tiredness never comes at all.

Tireless says in plain English what indefatigable says in Latin dress: the person does not grow weary, no matter how long the work runs. Being the everyday word, tireless fits small heroics — a tireless den mother — while indefatigable rolls a drum and suits effort on a grand, public scale.

Unflagging attaches to the effort rather than the person: unflagging energy, unflagging enthusiasm, support that never loses force or pace. Indefatigable describes the human being who supplies all of that — the campaigner or night nurse whom the work itself cannot wear down.

At mile eighty of the hundred-mile trail race, the pacers who had taken turns beside Ruiz were done — calves cramping, headlamps dimming, one asleep in a folding chair.
Ruiz's stride at mile ninety matched her stride at mile ten, and at the finish she asked, quite seriously, where breakfast was.
Her crew calls her indefatigable and schedules its own naps around the fact.
Indefatigable makes a stronger claim than hardworking or determined: not that the effort is great, but that the well it draws from never empties.
Inside the word sits de- + fatigare, 'to tire out completely' — negated.
This is the person the work cannot wear down, however long it runs.
Indefatigable is the long word you earn by never stopping — campaigners, archivists, nurses on doubled shifts.
Tireless says the same thing in plainer clothes; indefatigable adds a drumroll, so spend it on effort that genuinely never flags, not on one productive afternoon.

Dropped on a remote Chilean island with two crates and a promise of a ship in five months, the botanist Ana Quiroga set a schedule her notebooks record without comment: collecting at dawn, pressing plants till noon, a new ridge every afternoon.
On the day a storm flattened her tent, the notebook lists forty-one new specimens.
Her contemporaries called her indefatigable, and the letters of the resupply captains suggest they meant it literally: no one ever saw her rest.
The collection she came home with — eleven thousand sheets — anchored the island's flora for a century.
Asked late in life how she had kept the pace, she said only that the plants did not wait, so neither did she.
